items.summary_raw: Visioner BIG | 🇺🇦🇷🇺🇱🇾🇩🇿‼️‼️ Russia’s military supply routes to Africa face a major setback as two naval convoys reportedly halt their advance towards Libya following the sinking of the Russian corvette Merkury in Benghazi.  According to Reuters, two Russian military flotillas carrying vehicles and equipment have interrupted their journeys across the Mediterranean following the November 22 attack. One convoy, escorted by the Russian frigate Admiral Golovko, turned back near the Strait of Sicily on the day of the attack, while a second flotilla reportedly halted off the Algerian coast, according to Ukrainian military intelligence and a Middle Eastern security source.  The disruption exposes the vulnerability of Moscow’s maritime logistics in the Mediterranean. Beyond the loss of a warship, prolonged interruptions to military shipments could undermine Russia’s ability to sustain its military presence in Libya and support operations across Africa. items.summary_raw: Visioner BIG | 🇫🇷‼️‼️ France has officially commissioned the De Grasse nuclear-powered attack submarine, strengthening its naval combat capabilities.  According to the French Ministry of the Armed Forces and Veterans Affairs, Admiral Christophe Cluzel approved the submarine’s entry into active service on November 20, following sea trials that began in February. The Suffren-class submarine has a surface displacement of 4,700 tonnes and a submerged displacement of 5,300 tonnes. It measures 99.5 meters in length and 8.8 meters in diameter, can exceed 25 knots underwater and is powered by a 150 MW pressurized-water nuclear reactor. Its four 533 mm torpedo tubes accommodate a weapons load of up to 20 munitions, including F21 heavyweight torpedoes, Exocet SM39 anti-ship missiles and MdCN cruise missiles. The submarine can also carry a removable hangar for special operations underwater vehicles.  The commissioning of De Grasse strengthens France’s underwater warfare, intelligence-gathering and long-range precision strike capabilities, while supporting its ability to conduct independent naval operations in strategically important regions.  See the latest updates with us: @visionergeo tweet

items.title: Labour row over Rosebank deepens as dozens of MPs warn PM not to block oilfield
items.summary_raw:
Warning of ‘lights out for Labour in Scotland’ as Burnham faces choice between warring factions over North Sea drilling project

Dozens of Labour MPs in favour of Rosebank are putting pressure on the prime minister not to block the North Sea oilfield, warning that doing so could spell “lights out for Labour in Scotland”.

As many as 80 pro-drilling MPs are considering writing their own letter to Andy Burnham after nearly 100 of their colleagues called on the prime minister not to allow the project to proceed. Scottish Labour leader Michael Marra has also reiterated his support for Rosebank, cautioning that “working-class people in vocational jobs” were threatened by the decline of the North Sea basin.

items.title: Water levels fell sharply in world’s rivers and lakes in two hottest years on record, study finds
items.summary_raw:
Researchers say effects particularly felt in South America where levels plunged even as some areas had extreme rain

Extreme global heat caused an unprecedented decline in the water levels of lakes, rivers and reservoirs around the world in 2023 and 2024, an international study has found.

The analysis of global water systems, a collaboration led by the Chinese Academy of Sciences, found that the planet’s surface freshwater fell sharply during the two years, which were the hottest on record. Global river flows fell to about 5.7% below normal, while the water stored in lakes and reservoirs dropped by 9.5%. Together, this was the largest synchronised decline in surface water since at least 1991.

items.title: Record-breaking California tides cause major flooding of roads and businesses
items.summary_raw:
Beaches close as Los Angeles and La Jolla see all-time high tides and big waves batter landmark pier in Pacifica

Super El Niño weather brought record-breaking high tides up and down the California coast on Wednesday, sending seawater rushing into beachside communities and flooding roads and businesses.

As big waves battered the coast, the tip of a landmark pier in Pacifica, south of San Francisco, was slammed into the sea, local news outlets reported. The pier, which had once housed a favorite local cafe, had previously suffered structural damage and had been closed to the public, the San Francisco Chronicle reported, and collapsed after contact with ocean swells 12 times stronger than on an average November day.

Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre reportedly used a Russian oligarch as an intermediary before holding direct talks with Vladimir Putin on October 27. According to the report, the two Nordic leaders assured Putin that NATO had no intention of imposing a naval blockade on Russia. The diplomatic efforts reportedly followed warnings from Moscow that it was prepared to carry out preemptive nuclear strikes to protect its interests in the Baltic Sea.  The reported contacts highlight the growing danger of military escalation in the Baltic region. Russia’s nuclear threats have raised the stakes of any confrontation with NATO, while Finland and Norway appear to be seeking ways to prevent a direct clash without abandoning their security commitments. items.title: World has six consecutive days 2C above preindustrial levels for first time
items.summary_raw:
Daily global surface temperature hit record 2.24C above baseline levels on Monday and streak is forecast to continue

For the first time, the world has experienced six consecutive days of temperatures 2C warmer than preindustrial levels, the Guardian has learned.

This record hot streak, which is continuing, is too brief to signify that the upper range of the Paris climate agreement target has been breached, but scientists said it was an early indication of what is to come unless fossil fuel emissions are rapidly eliminated. It is also likely to feed into growing scientific concerns that global heating may be accelerating.

items.title: Bill McKibben: 2027 may be the year Americans turn on fossil fuels – Stateside with Kai and Carter
items.summary_raw:
It’s been another year in which the climate emergency has encroached on the lives of Americans across the country. From gigantic waves battering the California coastline to heat domes driving triple-digit temperatures in the southwest, we are reminded regularly that a crisis is here. Meanwhile, leaders gathered in Turkey for Cop31 failed to reach an agreement on how to move forward, and the US didn’t even bother to show up. To understand this moment, Kai Wright speaks to the environmentalist and author Bill McKibben about what he thinks must be done to slow the rapid advances of global heating, and what he wants to see from Democrats in 2027. Plus, he answers your questions about solar power, and how to talk to your family about the climate emergency

A group of more than 120 climate scientists have urged US lawmakers to not pass contentious legislation to speed up the building of energy projects, datacenters and other infrastructure, amid a growing backlash to the sweeping permitting bill.

In an open letter to members of the House of Representatives, the collection of Earth and social sciences researchers expressed “deep concern” that the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (or Baaja) weakens environmental laws, locks in new fossil fuel projects without recourse and delivers only minor cuts to planet-heating emissions.

I want us to remain that way, because I believe Christianity has helped shape us into a good society." - Open Source Intel tweet

items.title: A year of deadly floods and fires – and yet Cop31 still collapsed. When will our leaders grasp the scale of this crisis? | Bill McGuire
items.summary_raw:
Fossil fuel producers are choking off progress while we reap the whirlwind of our inaction. This is what sleepwalking to disaster looks like

It’s sometimes said that we are sleepwalking into climate catastrophe. But the reality is that we are walking into it with our eyes wide open, in the full knowledge that we are dooming the lives of our children, and countless generations down the line, to hell on Earth. In the UK, summer temperatures could hit the mid-40s within decades, making extreme drought and harvest failures the norm, and leaving people camping in the streets as houses become overheated death traps. Across Europe, the fastest-heating continent on the planet, the 50C temperature mark could be broken as soon as next year. Elsewhere, by 2050, humid heatwaves could take many thousands of lives in a single day in parts of China, South Asia and the Gulf region.

items.title: The Guardian view on Cop31: a just transition needs more than fine words | Editorial
items.summary_raw:
Petrostates blocked ambition while wealthy nations withheld cash support. The climate crisis demands the next UN summit turns promises into action

In a negotiation the maxim is usually that no deal is better than a bad deal. But the failure of Cop31 in Turkey to get a climate pact – the first time this has happened in 17 years – should not be an excuse for leaving the planet with the damaging status quo. A hard bargain needs a credible route to agreement: by making commitments, seeking concessions and getting others to reciprocate. This did not happen at the weekend.

Responsibility for the breakdown lay principally with petrostates resisting a transition away from fossil fuels and wealthy nations that are unwilling to finance it properly. With the US absent, the EU was foremost among the latter. European governments’ objection to fossil-fuel backsliding by a Saudi-Russian coalition was right, but

items.title: The good news out of Cop31? That most of the world’s governments said no to an agreement stripped of meaning | Bill Hare
items.summary_raw:
Co-chairing global climate talks is clearly not something to be repeated, certainly not by Australia, which is exporting climate pain

The failure of Cop31 in Antalya was a line in the sand moment, a victory for multiculturalism as countries stood up to the big fossil fuel producers and said no. The text they rejected barely recognised the catastrophic climate emergency we’re facing, let alone signalled a definitive move away from fossil fuels.

The good news is that most of the world’s governments rejected an agreement stripped of meaning. And the power of one particular fossil fuel producer, Saudi Arabia, needs particular scrutiny. What we also know is that co-chairing global climate talks is clearly not something to be repeated, certainly not by Australia. It didn’t work.

Two supertankers hit mines near Hormuz, Iranian navy says

Iran's navy said on Sunday that two supertankers hit naval mines and caught fire after entering a "restricted area" east of the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian media reported.

According to the Fars news agency, the navy said the tankers had switched off their detection and navigation systems and struck the mines north of Ghanam Island.

Both vessels reportedly stopped moving.

Supertankers usually carry two million barrels of oil or more, about twice as much as a standard tanker.

The navy also warned that relying on "smugglers such as CENTCOM", referring to US Central Command, would result in "nothing but heavy losses".

items.title: Cop31 ends in failure as countries reject climate deal over fossil fuels
items.summary_raw:
Cop31 ends in failure as countries reject climate deal over fossil fuels

The United Nations climate summit in Turkey became the longest-ever UN climate conference on Sunday as negotiations over a final agreement descended into deadlock, with the European Union and several other countries formally rejecting the proposed text.

The talks in Antalya, known as Cop31, continued more than 44 hours beyond their scheduled Friday conclusion, surpassing the previous record set by Cop25 in Madrid in 2019.

The latest draft, presented by the Turkish and Australian presidencies in an attempt to bridge divisions between countries, failed to secure consensus over its omission of explicit references to fossil fuels and disagreements over climate finance.

items.title: Turkey says Israel blocking thousands of container homes from entering Gaza
items.summary_raw:
Turkey says Israel blocking thousands of container homes from entering Gaza

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has said Israel is blocking thousands of container homes destined for Gaza, adding that Israeli authorities argue Hamas could use the metal structures  for manufacturing weapons.

Fidan told Turkish broadcaster TGRT Haber on Saturday that President Recep Tayyip Erdogan had ordered the temporary housing units, which Turkey used during the earthquake, to be sent to the Palestinian enclave.

He said Israeli restrictions were leaving displaced Palestinians dependent on fabric tents, exposing them to flooding, storms and cold weather.

“When floods, storms or cold weather come, they cause a disaster at least as devastating as hunger, if not more so,” he said.
